Camera Calibration 
Camera calibration is a fundamental step in computer vision and image processing that acts as the bridge between the 2D 
world of images and the 3D world of physical space. (Calibrate the camera means estimation of the projection matrix.)
The primary motivation is to understand and mathematically model how a camera transforms a 3D scene into a 2D grid of 
pixels. 
Without calibration, an image is just a collection of colored dots. With it, each dot becomes a precise geometric ray.
Why camera calibration is required –
1.Correction of lens distortion: Most camera lenses, especially wide-angle ones, do not project perfectly linear images. Light 
rays bend as they pass through the glass, leading to optical aberrations: like radial and tangential distortion. 
2. Estimating Intrinsic and external parameters: To perform any measurement or 3D reconstruction, we need to know the 
"internal" characteristics of the camera. Like focal length, principal point, skew coefficient.
3. Geometric 3D Reconstruction: 
The ultimate goal in many applications is to recover 3D information from 2D images. 
Calibration is motivated by the need to solve:
Visual SLAM: Allowing robots or drones to map their surroundings and navigate through them accurately.
Stereo vision: Using two cameras to calculate depth (triangulation). You cannot find the distance to an object if you don't know 
the exact geometric relationship between the two cameras.

Steps in contrast limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE).
The input image is divided into a grid of small, non-overlapping, and equally sized tiles.
The contrast enhancement is performed independently for each of these tiles.
For each tile, the pixel intensity histogram is computed.
Contrast Limiting: A clip limit is applied to each histogram bin. This limit, usually determined 
by the distribution of the histogram and a user-defined parameter, it prevents any single gray-
level bin from having too high a count.
Any pixel count in a histogram bin that exceeds the clip limit is clipped (or truncated) to that 
limit.
The total number of clipped pixels (the excess) is then redistributed evenly among all the 
histogram bins. This ensures that the overall brightness of the tile is maintained. This step is 
what distinguishes CLAHE from standard AHE and prevents noise over-amplification.
A local histogram equalization has 
been performed, after the histogram 
has been clipped and redistributed.

Edges represent boundaries of characters and are extracted using operators like Sobel or Canny. 
Characteristic points like corners, junctions, and endpoints of strokes are detected here.
Contours of the character are extracted to track boundaries and curves which can describe the 
overall geometry. 
Statistical measures like zoning (dividing the character into zones and calculating pixel densities), 
moments and projection profiles (horizontal/vertical pixel distributions) are computed. These 
capture global and local shape properties complementing geometric features.
Transformations such as Fourier descriptors, Wavelets, or Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) convert 
spatial pixel data into frequency or scale domains. Such features are powerful for capturing texture, 
periodicity, and invariant aspects of characters.
All extracted features are compiled into a fixed-length feature vector representing the 
character uniquely. This vector feeds directly into classifiers (e.g., SVM, neural networks) 
that perform the final character recognition.

Video formation 
A video is formed by sequencing a series of still images, called frames, and displaying them rapidly to create the illusion 
of continuous motion. This process is known as video formation and is grounded in the principle of persistence of vision, 
where the human eye perceives a fluid motion if frames are shown quickly enough—typically 24, 30, or 60 frames per 
second (fps).
•Capture: A video camera or imaging sensor captures a scene at discrete time intervals. Each individual capture at a moment 
is one frame—essentially a static image.
•Storage: These frames are then stored sequentially, initially as analog signals (in older systems) or immediately as digital 
data (in modern digital cameras).
•Rendering/Display: When played back, these frames are displayed in rapid succession at a specified fps on a screen. The 
human brain blends these into a perception of smooth, continuous motion.
•Encoding/Compression: Before a video is distributed or streamed, the sequence of frames is typically compressed using 
standards like MPEG, H.264, or HEVC. Compression leverages both spatial redundancy (within a frame) and temporal 
redundancy (between frames) to reduce file size.
•Playback: On playback devices, these frames are decoded and rendered back into a video stream for viewers.

Video Sampling 
Video sampling is the essential process of converting a continuous analog video signal into a discrete digital signal.
Temporal Sampling
Spatial Sampling
Spatial sampling refers to selecting discrete points 
across the two spatial dimensions—width and height—
of each video frame to create a grid of pixels.
Higher the spatial sampling rate, the more pixels per 
frame, as a result providing more detail.
A 1920x1080 HD frame is a result of sampling an image 
at 1920 horizontal and 1080 vertical points.
For high-resolution content, spatial sampling should 
satisfy the Nyquist criterion, ensuring the sampling 
frequency is at least twice the highest spatial frequency 
in the image to avoid loss of information and aliasing.
Temporal sampling refers to how often the scene is 
sampled over time, essentially determining how many 
frames per second (fps) are captured. This converts 
continuous motion into a series of discrete snapshots.
Cameras or video systems sample the scene at uniform 
intervals—commonly 24, 30, or 60 times per second.
Example: A standard film runs at 24 fps, meaning the scene 
is sampled 24 times every second.
Too low a temporal sampling rate causes motion artifacts 
like strobing or jerkiness (temporal aliasing).

Video Coding and Video Compression
Video Coding 
•
Video coding is the process of representing video data in a standardized digital format.
•
It converts uncompressed video (raw pixel data) into a bitstream following a specification like H.264, HEVC, or VP9.
•
 It ensures video can be interpreted accurately by decoders across diverse devices and applications.
Video Compression 
•
Video compression is the reduction of video data size by removing redundant information and exploiting similarities 
within and between frames. 
•
Compression is achieved through codecs (COder/DECoder), which use coding methods to minimize file size while 
maintaining visual quality.
•
Intraframe (Spatial) Compression: Compresses each frame individually by summarizing similar pixel regions—this 
addresses spatial redundancy.​
•
Interframe (Temporal) Compression: Stores only changes or differences between consecutive frames, exploiting 
temporal redundancy—this greatly improves compression efficiency for video streams.

46
Frame based Compression (MPEG) 
Frame-based compression in MPEG is a method that reduces both spatial and temporal redundancy in a video by 
encoding and arranging frames of different types within a group of pictures (GOP).
Frame-based compression, as used in MPEG (Moving Picture Experts Group) standards, encodes video frame by frame.
MPEG uses three types of frames:
• I-frames (Intra-coded): Encoded without reference to other frames.
• P-frames (Predicted): Encoded using data from previous frames.
• B-frames (Bi-directional): Encoded using both previous and future frames.
This combination allows MPEG to achieve high compression ratios while maintaining acceptable visual quality.

Size of the Pinhole 
Diffraction is a physical phenomenon where waves (such as light, 
sound, or water) bend, spread out, and interfere with each other when 
they encounter an obstacle or pass through a narrow opening.
When the pinhole is relatively large, light from a single point on an 
object passes through the hole and creates a large "spot" on the sensor. 
This is purely geometrical.
•The Result: The image is blurry because the spots (pixels) are too big 
and overlap.
As you keep making the pinhole smaller and smaller, you eventually reach a 
point where the hole is comparable to the wavelength of light. At this stage, 
light waves begin to hit the edges of the pinhole and "scatter" or bend 
inward.
Problem: Calculate the optimum pinhole diameter for a 
camera with an effective focal length of 50mm. assuming 
the wavelength of light is 550nm. 
Steps – 
Multiply focal length and wavelength 
 50 x 0.00055 = 0.0275 mm
Take the square root = sqrt(0.0275) = 0.16583
Multiply by the constant = 2 x 0.16583 = 0.33166mm
Optimum pinhole diameter is 0.33mm
If the hole is larger than 0.33 mm: Light rays from a single point on 
the object will spread out too much before hitting the sensor, creating a 
blurry "circle of confusion."
If the hole is smaller than 0.33 mm: The wave nature of light 
causes it to bend (diffract) around the edges of the hole, which also 
creates a blurry image.

Motivation : Visual quality of image may be hampered by illumination condition or wrong setting of camera sensor. 
To rectify the same, one can utilized power law transformation or Gamma Corrections. Basic idea is to raise the pixel

Case 1: Dark Pixel (r = 7) with gamma = 0.5
gamma < 1, we expect this pixel to become significantly brighter.
1.Normalize: 7 / 255 = 0.02745
2.Apply Gamma: (0.02745)^{0.5} = 0.16568
3.Scale back: 0.16568 x 255 = 42.25
Result: The pixel value jumps from 7 to 42. This "stretches" the dark detail, making it much more visible.
Case 2: Bright Pixel (r = 240) with gamma = 1.5
gamma > 1, we expect this pixel to become darker. 
1.Normalize: (240 / 255 ) = 0.94118$
2.Apply Gamma: (0.94118)^{1.5} = 0.91354
3.Scale back: 0.91354 x 255 = 232.95 
Result: The pixel value drops from 240 to 233. Even though it is a small numerical drop, in an image, this helps reduce "blowout" and adds 
depth to highlight areas.
In image processing, we almost always prefer Gamma Corrections over Log/Exponential because of its tunability by varying the gamma

Sensitivity to Noise
The Problem: If your center pixel is 80 and a neighbor is 79, the bit is 0. If noise changes that neighbor to 81, the bit flips to 1.
The Result: A "smooth" texture can suddenly look like a "noisy" texture in the histogram just because of a slight sensor grain.

The Result: LBP gives both of these a "1." The algorithm cannot distinguish between a very soft, subtle gradient and a sharp, high-contrast edge. This is

Gabor Filter: 
A Gabor filter is a linear filter used to detect whether an image has specific frequency content in specific directions. It is modeled after the way 
the human visual cortex processes information—our brains are naturally tuned to detect edges and stripes at various angles and scales.
Mathematically, a Gabor filter is a Gaussian kernel (a blur) multiplied by a Sinusoidal plane wave (a set of stripes).
•The Sinusoid: This acts as the "detector" for a specific frequency (fineness/coarseness) and orientation (angle).
•The Gaussian: This "localizes" the detector, so it only looks at a small window of the image at a time, rather than the whole thing at once.

54
Gabor Filter
Five key parameters of Gabor filter 
To "tune" a Gabor filter to find a specific texture, you adjust these parameters:
1.Lambda (Wavelength): Defines the width of the stripes. 
 If Small lambda 
 finds fine textures (sand); 
 large lambda 
 finds coarse textures (large bricks).
2. Theta (Orientation): 
 Defines the angle of the stripes 
 (e.g. 0 degree for horizontal, 
 90 degree for vertical).
3.(Phase Offset): 
 Determines the position of the stripes relative to the center.
4. Sigma : Controls the size of the Gaussian envelope (the "look area").
5. Gamma (Aspect Ratio): Controls how circular or elliptical the filter is
How it is Utilized for Texture Analysis
Unlike LBP, which gives you one histogram, Gabor filters are 
almost always used in a Filter Bank.
Step A: Create a Filter Bank
Because one filter only detects one specific angle and size, you 
create a "bank" of many filters (e.g., 5 scales x 8 orientations = 40 
filters).
Step B: Convolution
You slide (convolve) every filter in the bank across the image. 
Each filter will "light up" (give a high response) only when it 
passes over a texture that matches its specific angle and frequency.
•Example: A 45 degree 
filter will show high values on the 
diagonal threads of a piece of fabric but will stay "dark" on 
horizontal lines.
Step C: Feature Extraction
After filtering, you don't keep the whole filtered image. Instead, 
you calculate Energy Measures (like Mean or Variance) for each 
of the 40 filtered results. These 40 numbers become the "Feature 
Vector" that describes the texture.
Step D: Provide these feature vector to NN or SVM..etc.
